title: How do you design and choose databases for microservices (database-per-service, SQL vs NoSQL vs Redis, scalability/consistency factors)?
shortTitle: How to design and choose databases for microservices

s1_definition.profdef: Designing databases for microservices means applying the database-per-service pattern — each service privately owns its data and schema, and no other service touches that storage directly — and then choosing the storage technology per service based on its access pattern and consistency needs rather than forcing one database on the whole system. You pick a relational store (PostgreSQL, Oracle) for strongly-consistent transactional data, a document or wide-column NoSQL store (MongoDB, Cassandra) for high-volume, flexible-schema, horizontally-scaled data, and an in-memory store (Redis) for caching, counters, and ephemeral low-latency data, letting each service use the engine that best fits its workload — an approach called polyglot persistence.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India as many departments. The core ledger that holds Rajesh's and Priya's actual balances needs strict, double-entry, never-wrong bookkeeping — that is a relational database, like a locked ledger book where every entry must balance. The audit department that stores billions of log events, where the shape of each event varies and nobody updates old entries, is happy with a NoSQL store — like a giant warehouse of filing cabinets you only ever add to. And the teller's quick note of "Rajesh's balance a moment ago" so the next screen loads instantly is a sticky note on the desk that you throw away after thirty seconds — that is Redis. Each department keeps its own records; no department reaches into another's cabinet.
s1_definition.oneliner: Give every service its own private database and choose that database by the service's workload — relational for correctness, NoSQL for scale and flexibility, Redis for speed.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Designing databases for microservices means applying the database-per-service pattern — each service privately owns its data and schema, and no other service touches that storage directly — and then choosing the storage technology per service based on its access pattern and consistency needs rather than forcing one database on the whole system. You pick a relational store (PostgreSQL, Oracle) for strongly-consistent transactional data, a document or wide-column NoSQL store (MongoDB, Cassandra) for high-volume, flexible-schema, horizontally-scaled data, and an in-memory store (Redis) for caching, counters, and ephemeral low-latency data, letting each service use the engine that best fits its workload — an approach called polyglot persistence.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of National Bank of India as many departments. The core ledger that holds Rajesh's and Priya's actual balances needs strict, double-entry, never-wrong bookkeeping — that is a relational database, like a locked ledger book where every entry must balance. The audit department that stores billions of log events, where the shape of each event varies and nobody updates old entries, is happy with a NoSQL store — like a giant warehouse of filing cabinets you only ever add to. And the teller's quick note of "Rajesh's balance a moment ago" so the next screen loads instantly is a sticky note on the desk that you throw away after thirty seconds — that is Redis. Each department keeps its own records; no department reaches into another's cabinet.

**One line to remember:** Give every service its own private database and choose that database by the service's workload — relational for correctness, NoSQL for scale and flexibility, Redis for speed.

sections.s2_technical:
The foundation is the database-per-service pattern. Each microservice owns its data exclusively; other services may read or change that data only by calling the owning service's API or by consuming its events — never by connecting to its database. This gives independent deployability (you can change the accounts schema without coordinating with ten teams), loose coupling, fault isolation (one database's problems do not cascade), and the freedom to pick the best engine per service. The cost is that data is now distributed, so cross-service joins and distributed transactions are no longer available, and you handle consistency with Sagas, events, and eventual consistency instead.

Choosing the engine comes down to the access pattern. Use a relational SQL database when you need strong consistency, ACID transactions, and complex relationships — the core ledger, accounts, and transfers where a lost or duplicated rupee is unacceptable and the data is highly structured. SQL gives you foreign keys, multi-row transactions, and expressive queries, at the cost of harder horizontal scaling (you scale up, add read replicas, or eventually shard).

Use a NoSQL database when scale, write throughput, flexible schema, or geographic distribution matters more than cross-entity transactions. A document store like MongoDB suits data naturally shaped as self-contained documents (a customer profile with nested preferences). A wide-column store like Cassandra suits massive write-heavy, time-series or event data (transaction history, audit logs) with tunable consistency and linear horizontal scaling across nodes. NoSQL typically trades strong consistency and joins for availability and partition tolerance, which you reason about through the CAP theorem — under a network partition you choose consistency or availability, and most AP stores give you eventual consistency.

Use Redis, an in-memory store, for anything that must be extremely fast and is either a cache or inherently ephemeral: cached balances with a short TTL, rate-limit counters, session data, leaderboards, and distributed locks. Redis is not usually your source of truth; it sits in front of the real database with a strategy like cache-aside (check Redis, on a miss read the database and populate Redis) and a TTL so stale data self-corrects.

A senior engineer frames the decision with a few factors. Consistency: does a wrong or stale value cause financial harm (then SQL and strong consistency) or is eventual consistency acceptable (then NoSQL)? Scale and throughput: thousands of writes per second with simple access patterns pushes you toward a horizontally-scalable NoSQL store. Query complexity: rich ad-hoc queries and joins favor SQL; simple key-based lookups favor key-value or document stores. Data shape and volatility: rigid, relational, long-lived data favors SQL; flexible, append-mostly, huge-volume data favors NoSQL. Latency: microsecond reads of hot data favor Redis as a cache. The right system is usually polyglot — the core transfer service on PostgreSQL, the transaction-history service on Cassandra, the profile service on MongoDB, and Redis caching in front of the read-heavy ones. A crucial rule: use NoSQL because the access pattern fits, not to avoid writing SQL, and never put money that must balance into an eventually-consistent store.
sections.s3_banking:
The real problem: National Bank of India is splitting a monolith into microservices and must decide where each kind of data lives. Three very different data needs show up, and forcing them into one shared database would be a mistake.

Problem 1 — The core transfer between Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001) must debit one and credit the other atomically; a half-done transfer that loses money is catastrophic. This demands ACID transactions and strong consistency. This is exactly what a relational SQL database provides, so the Account/Transfer service uses PostgreSQL.

Problem 2 — Every transfer produces a history record, and the bank keeps billions of them, written constantly, queried by account and time, never updated. Cross-account joins are unnecessary. This is a write-heavy, append-only, huge-volume pattern, which is exactly where a horizontally-scalable NoSQL store like Cassandra shines, so the Transaction-History service uses NoSQL.

Problem 3 — The mobile app shows Rajesh's balance on every screen; hitting PostgreSQL for each view wastes the precious transactional database. A short-lived cached copy is enough. This is exactly the caching pattern, so a Redis cache-aside layer sits in front of balance reads with a thirty-second TTL.

What the code will do: a runnable demo models polyglot persistence with three simple in-memory stand-ins that behave like the three engines. `RelationalAccountStore` enforces ACID-style atomic transfer (both debit and credit succeed or neither does). `NoSqlHistoryStore` appends history documents with flexible shape and no joins. `RedisCache` caches balances with a TTL and demonstrates cache-aside with hit and miss. `BankingFacade.transfer()` ties them together: perform the atomic transfer in SQL, append a history document to NoSQL, and invalidate the Redis cache. A `readBalance()` method shows a cache miss (reads SQL, populates Redis) followed by a cache hit.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile and run the demo
javac PolyglotBankingDemo.java
java PolyglotBankingDemo

# In the real platform each service is built and deployed independently:
# account-service (PostgreSQL)
mvn -pl account-service clean package
# history-service (Cassandra)
mvn -pl history-service clean package

# Spin up the three engines locally
docker run -d --name pg       -e POSTGRES_DB=accountdb -p 5432:5432 postgres:16
docker run -d --name cassandra -p 9042:9042 cassandra:5
docker run -d --name redis    -p 6379:6379 redis:7
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a transfer of Rs.50000 from Rajesh (SAV2001, Rs.1,000,000) to Priya (CUR3001, Rs.250,000), then two balance reads of SAV2001, then a deliberately oversized transfer.

Step 1: `BankingFacade.transfer()` calls `RelationalAccountStore.atomicTransfer()`. Inside one simulated ACID transaction, Rajesh is debited to Rs.950,000 and Priya credited to Rs.300,000. Both legs commit together. The money, which must never be wrong, lives in the strongly-consistent SQL store.

Step 2: Two history documents are appended to the NoSQL store — a DEBIT document for SAV2001 and a CREDIT document for CUR3001. These are pure writes with flexible shape, no joins, no transaction, which is why a horizontally-scalable NoSQL engine is the right home.

Step 3: The facade evicts the cached balances for both accounts from Redis so stale values cannot be served after the transfer.

Step 4: The first `readBalance("SAV2001")` is a cache miss. Redis has nothing, so the facade reads the source of truth in SQL (Rs.950,000), populates Redis with a thirty-second TTL, and returns it.

Step 5: The second `readBalance("SAV2001")` is a cache hit. Redis still has the value within its TTL, so it returns Rs.950,000 instantly without touching the transactional database — exactly the latency win Redis provides.

Step 6: The oversized transfer from Priya is attempted. The debit fails because of insufficient funds, the SQL store rolls back both legs, and balances remain unchanged. No history is appended and no cache is corrupted. ACID atomicity in the relational store protected the money.

Final output:

```
11:05:10 INFO    [SQL] COMMIT SAV2001 1000000->950000, CUR3001 250000->300000
11:05:10 INFO    [NoSQL] appended history DEBIT Rs.50000 acct=SAV2001
11:05:10 INFO    [NoSQL] appended history CREDIT Rs.50000 acct=CUR3001
11:05:10 INFO    [Redis MISS] read SQL, cached balance SAV2001 = Rs.950000
11:05:10 INFO    [Redis HIT] balance SAV2001 = Rs.950000
11:05:10 WARNING [SQL] ROLLBACK — no money moved
11:05:10 SEVERE  transfer rejected: insufficient funds in CUR3001 (balances unchanged)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  transfer(SAV2001 → CUR3001, Rs.50000)
    │
    ▼
  BankingFacade.transfer()
    ├─► RelationalAccountStore.atomicTransfer()   [PostgreSQL — ACID, strong]
    │       SAV2001 1,000,000 → 950,000
    │       CUR3001   250,000 → 300,000   COMMIT (both or neither)
    │
    ├─► NoSqlHistoryStore.append() ×2             [Cassandra — append-only, scalable]
    │       {accountId, DEBIT/CREDIT, amount, ts}  no join, no txn
    │
    └─► RedisCache.evict(balance:SAV2001/CUR3001) [Redis — keep cache fresh]

  readBalance(SAV2001)
    │
    ├─ cache MISS → read PostgreSQL (950,000) → put Redis (TTL 30s)
    └─ cache HIT  → return 950,000 from Redis (microseconds, DB untouched)

  transfer(CUR3001 → SAV2001, Rs.9,999,999)
    │ debit fails (insufficient) → SQL ROLLBACK → balances unchanged, no history
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Choosing & Wiring Storage per Service ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Database-per-Service: each service owns its schema               │
  │ Polyglot Persistence: SQL + NoSQL + Redis by workload            │
  │ Cache-Aside: check Redis → miss → DB → populate Redis            │

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: each store class handles one storage concern                  │
  │ O: add a new store (e.g. search) without changing existing ones  │
  │ D: facade depends on store abstractions, not concrete engines    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ┌───────────────────────────┐
  │ BankingFacade             │
  │ - sql:   RelationalStore  │───▶ RelationalAccountStore (ACID)
  │ - nosql: NoSqlHistoryStore│───▶ NoSqlHistoryStore (append-only)
  │ - cache: RedisCache       │───▶ RedisCache (TTL, cache-aside)
  │ + transfer(from,to,amt)   │
  │ + readBalance(id):BigDec  │
  └───────────────────────────┘

  ── Decision Table (which engine) ────────────────────────────────
  need ACID + money correctness ........... PostgreSQL (SQL)
  write-heavy, append-only, huge volume .... Cassandra (NoSQL)
  flexible document, nested profile ........ MongoDB (NoSQL)
  hot read, ephemeral, counters ............ Redis (in-memory)

  ── Call Chain ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
  1. Facade.transfer(SAV2001, CUR3001, 50000)
  2.   → sql.atomicTransfer()      COMMIT or ROLLBACK
  3.   → nosql.append(DEBIT) ; append(CREDIT)
  4.   → cache.evict(both balances)
  5. Facade.readBalance(SAV2001)
  6.   → cache.get() MISS → sql.balanceOf() → cache.put(TTL 30s)
  7.   → cache.get() HIT  → return from Redis
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Designing databases for microservices starts with one non-negotiable principle: database-per-service. Each service privately owns its data and schema, and no other service ever connects to that database directly — other services get the data only through the owning service's API or by consuming its events. That gives me independent deployability, loose coupling, and fault isolation, and it is what makes polyglot persistence possible, because once each service owns its store, I am free to choose the best engine for that service's workload instead of forcing one database on everyone. The trade-off I always acknowledge is that data is now distributed, so cross-service joins and distributed transactions disappear, and I handle consistency with Sagas, events, and eventual consistency.

Choosing the engine is driven by the access pattern, and I reason through a few factors: consistency needs, scale and write throughput, query complexity, data shape, and latency. I use a relational database like PostgreSQL when correctness is paramount and I need ACID transactions and relationships — the core ledger, accounts, and transfers, where a lost or duplicated rupee is unacceptable. I use a NoSQL database when scale, write volume, flexible schema, or geographic distribution matter more than cross-entity transactions — a wide-column store like Cassandra for massive append-only transaction history, or a document store like MongoDB for self-contained records like customer profiles. And I use Redis for anything that must be extremely fast and is either a cache or inherently ephemeral — cached balances with a short TTL, rate-limit counters, sessions, and distributed locks — always as a layer in front of the real source of truth, never as the source of truth itself.

I put this into practice when we broke up a monolith at National Bank of India. The transfer between Rajesh and Priya has to debit one and credit the other atomically, so the account service sits on PostgreSQL with real ACID transactions; a failed transfer rolls back cleanly and no money moves. Every transfer also produces history records, and we keep billions of them, written constantly, queried by account and time, never updated and never joined, so the history service sits on Cassandra, which scales horizontally and absorbs that write load. And because the mobile app shows a balance on every screen, we put Redis in front of balance reads with a thirty-second TTL using cache-aside, so a cache miss reads PostgreSQL once and every subsequent read for half a minute is served from memory, sparing the transactional database.

The senior nuances I raise are these. Reason about consistency honestly through the CAP theorem — under a network partition an AP NoSQL store gives you availability with eventual consistency, which is fine for history but never for money. Choose NoSQL because the access pattern genuinely fits, not to avoid writing SQL. Scale SQL first with read replicas and connection pooling before reaching for sharding. And keep Redis as a cache with a TTL so stale data self-corrects, invalidating it on writes so you never serve a balance that is wrong after a transfer.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is this: give every service its own private database, then choose that database by the workload — relational for transactional correctness, NoSQL for scale and flexible high-volume data, and Redis for hot, ephemeral, low-latency data — because the right architecture is polyglot, matching each engine to what that service actually does.
